content:
Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the latest launch of a more affordable non-designer version are both marketed with built-in AI features, but in early July the company announced what can only be described as "outrageous" limits on the free usage of an accessibility feature.

In effect, Meta has retroactively placed a paywall on a hardware product already sold to customers. Update: The social network now says it has "paused" plans to put the feature behind a paywall — see end of story.

Meta first began rolling out the Conversation Focus feature last December.

It is a clever application of AI, with one major advantage being that it runs on-device, meaning it neither impacts privacy nor requires mobile data.

However, according to a report by The Verge, Meta is now imposing a cap on the number of free uses of this feature.

This is particularly unacceptable. Firstly, as the publication's reporter Sean Hollister pointed out, the feature runs on the device and does not use Meta's servers, so there is absolutely no reason to charge users for it. Secondly, this is an accessibility feature, and some users may have specifically purchased these glasses precisely for this reason.

Top-rated comment posted by KJ705

Hard to imagine putting an accessibility feature behind a paywall will end well.

On the topic of accessibility: I recently bought AirPods Pro 3 for my mother specifically to use as a hearing aid. The hearing aid feature is extremely impressive, but I wish it did a better job at cancelling background noise. She finds it very useful.

When The Verge reached out to Meta for comment, Meta replied that the restrictions currently only apply to the Conversation Focus feature, hinting that other AI features may also have usage limits imposed in the future. The company told this paper that since the feature is designed for people with normal hearing, it does not consider it an accessibility feature. But I feel this is just sophistry, because in noisy environments, some people do have more difficulty following conversations.

All of this may be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses — it gives consumers another reason to choose AI smart glasses from a manufacturer with a better reputation, even if the upfront cost may be higher. Apple has always stressed that it never seeks a return on investment on accessibility features, but rather views them as a contribution to building a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to launch sometime next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge that it has paused plans to limit the Conversation Focus feature, but has not abandoned the idea of putting some glasses features behind a paywall in the future.
